newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada Dec consumer prices rise 2.2 percent.
newsitem.headline: Canada Dec consumer prices rise 2.2 percent.

text.p: Canada's unadjusted December Consumer Price Index was unchanged from November and rose 2.2 percent from a year earlier, Statistics Canada said on Thursday.
The government agency said the CPI rose 1.6 percent in 1996 from 1995. The agency calculates the annual average index by averaging the indices for the twelve months of the calendar year.
Analysts said the trend toward slight increases in the CPI was an indication that Canada's economy is gradually picking up speed, but that any interest rate increases were unlikely at this time.
"This is just another indication that the economy has turned the corner," said Doug Porter, senior economist at Nesbitt Burns Inc.
Analysts also said a slightly higher consumer inflation rate meant the Bank of Canada would pursue a steady monetary policy, in contrast with the aggressive easing of the past year and a half.

"Certainly with the underpinning that we are getting a bit of inflation out of the U.S., I would say the bias is up here in terms of core rates and overall CPI," said Mark Mullins, chief economist at Midland Walwyn. "All that is simply to say there is simply no more room for monetary easing."

A Reuters survey of economists had forecast the seasonally adjusted CPI to fall 0.3 percent for the month and the undadjusted CPI to rise 0.2 percent. The survey also forecast a 1.95 percent increase in the all-items year-over-year index.

Statistics Canada said annual increases in the CPI have remained at low and steady levels since 1992, ranging from 0.2 percent in 1994 to 2.1 percent in 1995. These increases were the smallest since the early 1960s.

The year-over-year increase in December was largely due to higher transportation charges, as well as higher prices for food, university tuition, telephone charges, rented accommodation and fuel oil prices.
The December inflation rate was higher than the 2.0 percent and 1.8 percent year-over-year increases posted in November and October.
"The acceleration of inflation since September was due primarily to increases in the rates for auto insurance, gasoline, air fares and food," Statistics Canada said.

There was no change in consumer prices in December from November as higher prices for air travel, tobacco products, natural gas and fuel oil were offset by declines in the cost of clothing and footwear, food from stores and traveller accommodation.
